name: capability-query
intent: Ask an object at runtime whether it supports a named optional interface or capability and return a usable handle (or an explicit negative) so callers invoke the contract they need without testing a concrete type, class name or version flag.
problem: A collaborator is exposed through a base or minimal interface, but an open-world caller may need an operation that only some implementations provide - flushing, seeking, rendering, cancellation or an extension hook. Concrete-type tests and casts couple the caller to implementations and require edits for each new type; one fat interface or a versioned capability bitmask instead makes absence ambiguous, so unsupported operations surface as exceptions, crashes or silent protocol drift rather than a deliberate fallback.
context: Use the pattern when support differs per object within one abstraction (optional interfaces, extension points, or interfaces added after implementers shipped), when the concrete type is unknown at a plugin or cross-module boundary, and when absence is an ordinary outcome. Keep the negotiated capability set stable for the object's lifetime unless the protocol explicitly provides versioned refresh semantics.
benefits: Callers depend on the capability interface they actually use, not on concrete classes: a new implementation joins the system without touching any query site.

Absence is an explicit, handled outcome - null, None, nil, Optional, a false ok flag - so the caller must design a fallback instead of discovering the problem as a ClassCastException or a segmentation fault.

Optional capabilities can be added to an existing abstraction without forcing every implementer to provide them (interface segregation): an implementation that predates the interface honestly answers 'no' rather than failing at the first call.
The capability can be selected as data at runtime - a Class token, a TypeId, a GUID, an interface id - which plain virtual dispatch cannot express.
Negotiation is separated from use: the client asks once, then calls the handle at full speed (COM states this separation as the reason QueryInterface exists).
Narrow capability interfaces keep authority small: holding the handle grants exactly the operations of that interface and nothing else, which is the basis of capability-based security.
tradeoffs: Every optional capability adds a branch plus a fallback at each call site; a codebase that queries frequently pays a per-capability tax that plain virtual dispatch does not.

Excessive queries indicate a broken abstraction (Dewhurst's Item 27 and More C++ Idioms both warn about this): if most call sites cast before calling, the operation belongs in the base interface, not behind a query.

Runtime checks cost: dynamic_cast cross-casts walk the class graph, and reflective tests (Class.isInstance, Type.IsAssignableFrom) are far slower than a virtual call - COM's rules even forbid ACL checks inside QueryInterface and require clients to cache the interface pointers they obtain.

Identity and lifetime become part of the contract: the returned handle may be a different pointer or object than the queried one (COM aggregation), so caching, equality and reference counting must be specified - hence COM's reflexive, symmetric and transitive rules.

The answer set must stay stable per object; a capability that appears or disappears between calls invalidates the caller's cached decision, which is why COM requires the interface set to be static, not dynamic.

In dynamic languages a positive answer is only about names: Python's runtime_checkable isinstance checks that members exist but not their signatures, and Ruby's respond_to? can be true for a method that raises on the current platform - the call remains the only real test.

Capability soup is the failure mode: adding a query for every incidental method leaves callers assembling undocumented combinations; define cohesive role interfaces and promote a capability to the base contract when most clients require it.

participants.responsibility: Needs functionality that only some implementations provide and must keep working (or degrade deliberately) when they do not; asks the capability question instead of assuming a concrete type.
The queried object: it owns the answer, decides which capabilities it exposes, and returns a usable handle on success or an explicit negative on failure.
The narrow optional interface whose support is being queried - one purpose per interface, kept free of members the implementer may not support.

The language or framework facility that performs the test and yields the handle: a dynamic_cast cross-cast, a type assertion, a type pattern, a Class/Type token test, QueryInterface(id), respond_to?/hasattr-style reflection, or a declared accessor.
What the client does with a negative answer: a simpler interface, a default or no-op behaviour, a diagnostic, or a hard error reported to its own caller.

use_cases: Framework and plugin hosts whose loaded components may additionally implement optional interfaces: net/http's Flusher, Hijacker and CloseNotifier on a ResponseWriter, io.Copy's WriterTo/ReaderFrom fast paths, COM's IUnknown::QueryInterface navigation.

Bridges and adapters across versions: an interface added after the implementation shipped must be able to answer 'no' safely instead of failing at the first call (Dewhurst's Checked Bridge; COM's motivation for E_NOINTERFACE).
Rich domain or document models where per-instance behaviours (renderable, serializable, approvable, closable) are attached to a few instances instead of the class.
Tooling and diagnostic paths over heterogeneous collections: checking for __len__/Sized, Symbol.iterator, respond_to?(:to_h) or a Seekable capability before choosing an algorithm.

Capability-based security and sandbox APIs, where holding the handle is the authorization: the query is how a client negotiates for the narrowest capability it needs (membranes and revocable forwarders build on it).
Runtime feature detection of an environment rather than a class (typeof window.fetch === 'function'): the same question asked of a platform surface before a call is attempted.

AI agent tool registration and tool selection: an agent runtime queries registered tools for optional capabilities (e.g., streaming, batch execution, cancellation) before invoking them, degrading gracefully when a tool lacks a requested capability.

LLM function-calling schemas where a model must declare which optional parameters or capabilities a tool supports; the runtime queries the tool's manifest before populating the function signature or routing a request.

RAG pipeline component negotiation: a retriever component is typed by a base interface, but a caller needs hybrid search (vector + BM25), streaming responses, or document-level metadata; the pipeline queries the component for the optional interface and falls back to a basic retrieval when the capability is absent.

Multi-agent system task routing: a supervisor holds references to worker agents typed by a common Agent interface; it queries each worker for optional capabilities (code execution, web search, file access) before assigning a task that requires a specific capability.

Go's net/http ResponseController probes optional Flush, Hijack, deadline and full-duplex methods through ResponseWriter wrappers, returning ErrNotSupported when a capability is not exposed rather than requiring a concrete writer type.

Java's ServiceLoader plugin boundary locates zero or more providers behind a service interface and lets applications inspect provider metadata before instantiation, so an empty or unsuitable capability set is handled without naming implementation classes.

LLVM's isa<T>/dyn_cast<T> casting framework asks IR and AST nodes whether they satisfy a capability predicate (classof) without hardware RTTI: dyn_cast yields a typed handle or null and every compiler pass branches its fallback path from that negative answer.

Qt's qobject_cast<T*> negotiates capabilities over QObject graphs through the meta-object system - event and slot code queries a generic QObject pointer for the widget interface it needs, gets nullptr when absent, and works across dynamic library boundaries without C++ RTTI.

Mozilla XPCOM's nsISupports::QueryInterface(iid) is the runtime interface-discovery root of every Firefox component: callers request an interface by UUID, receive NS_NOINTERFACE when a component predates or lacks one, and release the returned pointer when done.
avoid_when: The capability can be required statically - put it in the base interface, a generic bound or a trait bound and let the compiler prove it; a runtime query there only moves a compile error into a branch.
The set of variants is closed and known - a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive matching, an enum or a dispatch table expresses the same decision with compiler-checked coverage.
The caller needs behaviour, not a handle - a default interface method, a no-op implementation (Null Object) or an ordinary virtual call removes the query entirely.
The type is known at construction time - inject the concrete capability once (Strategy/composition) instead of querying on every call.
The check would be an authorization decision - permission must follow from holding a handle, not from asking whether an interface exists (COM forbids ACL checks inside QueryInterface).
You are about to query inside a hot loop - resolve the handle once, cache it and keep the question out of the inner path.

A stable boolean feature flag fully describes a capability with no associated handle or lifetime; use the documented flag, and reserve interface negotiation for operations, identity or ownership that the flag cannot express.

Independently deployed peers share an unversioned bitmask or string list; unknown flags can be misread as supported operations, so use versioned identifiers with an explicit unknown-capability fallback.
anti_patterns: Type tags instead of capabilities: branching on a class-name string or an exact type equality test - it fails for subclasses, wrappers and proxies that do support the interface, and needs editing for every new type.
Query-then-cast without a fallback: the negative answer is treated as impossible, so the branch that should degrade is an assertion, a cast or an empty else.
Querying in a loop: re-asking on every iteration (or for every element of a collection) instead of caching the handle or the decision.
One capability interface with isSupported(name) plus do(name, args): the types are erased and the pattern's safety is gone - capability interfaces exist so the compiler can see the operations.
Casting the queried handle to a concrete implementation right after a successful query: the capability was the contract, and the concrete cast puts the coupling back.
Using the query as a permission check (COM's own rules state that QueryInterface must never check ACLs).

Morphing interface: returning the same pointer for multiple incompatible interfaces based on query order - violates COM's reflexive, symmetric and transitive rules and causes memory corruption when callers use the returned pointer under the wrong interface's calling convention.

Capability soup: adding one query for every incidental operation -> clients assemble undocumented combinations and every wrapper must forward a growing matrix -> define cohesive role interfaces, and promote a capability to the base contract once it is a common invariant.
design_principles: Interface segregation: capabilities are narrow, single-purpose interfaces, never one fat interface with half-supported members.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: the caller depends only on the capability it negotiated for.
Open/closed principle: new implementations and new optional capabilities arrive without edits at existing call sites.
Explicit failure: a missing capability is a value (null/Optional/false/error), not an exception raised later by a bad cast.
Least authority: the handle returned by the query grants exactly the operations of that capability and nothing more (the foundation of capability-based security).
Separation of negotiation from use: ask once for the capability, then call the handle (COM states this as the design reason for QueryInterface).

Static interface set: the answer to a capability query must not change for the lifetime of the object - cached results are only valid because the interface set is immutable per instance (COM's rule, violated by dynamic capability discovery that can appear and disappear).
best_practices: Keep capability interfaces narrow and cohesive: one question asks for one capability, and the handle exposes only that capability's operations.
Always design the negative path: decide what the caller does when the answer is no, and make that behaviour part of the capability's documented contract.
Make the answer set stable for the object's lifetime so results and handles can be cached (reflexive, symmetric and transitive wherever the runtime supports it).
Cache the handle (or the negative answer) instead of re-querying in hot paths, and document the lifetime, ownership and identity of what the query returns.
Query the capability, never the class: no class-name switches, no exact-type comparisons.
Do not use capability queries for access control; authorize the handle, not the question (COM: QueryInterface must never check ACLs).
Prefer the static route - base interface, generic/trait bound, sealed variants - whenever the capability set is known at compile time, and keep runtime queries for genuinely open extension points.
In dynamic languages, treat the actual method call as the only reliable capability test: respond_to? and hasattr confirm a name, not a compatible signature or runtime behaviour.

When a capability interface is added to a system after some implementations already exist, design the query to return a negative answer (not an exception or crash) for legacy implementations - this is the COM versioning guarantee that old objects safely answer 'no' to new interface queries.

Distinguish capability negotiation (the query itself) from capability transport (how the handle is passed or stored): the handle's lifetime and reference-counting semantics must be documented separately from the query contract.

For AI agent tool registries and similar dynamic discovery scenarios, treat the capability manifest as a static declaration made at registration time; do not re-query the running tool for capabilities that were not declared in its manifest.

related_patterns_notes.object-capability-model: object-capability-model Object-Capability Model makes possession of an object the authority boundary; Capability Query can obtain a narrow object but must not replace authorization with an ACL check.
related_patterns_notes.capability-based-security: capability-based-security Capability-Based Security treats an unforgeable handle as authority, while Capability Query is a general negotiation pattern that is not itself an access-control mechanism.
related_patterns_notes.role-object: Role Object gives one entity a context-specific view or role, while Capability Query negotiates that view or another narrow interface at runtime when support is optional.
related_patterns_notes.extension-object: Extension Object stores optional behavior in separately obtained extension objects; Capability Query is the negotiation step that obtains the extension handle without exposing concrete classes.
related_patterns_notes.type-erasure: Type Erasure hides the concrete representation while preserving a chosen contract, whereas Capability Query discovers which additional contract can safely be used.
related_patterns_notes.marker-interface: A Marker Interface communicates membership without operations; Capability Query should normally return a usable, narrow interface rather than a tag that still requires a cast.
related_patterns_notes.interface-class: Interface Class defines the optional contract, while Capability Query is the runtime selection mechanism for an implementation that exposes that contract.
related_patterns_notes.dynamic-proxy: Dynamic Proxy intercepts or forwards calls through a substitute object; Capability Query asks whether that object or its unwrapped target exposes a particular contract.
related_patterns_notes.null-object: Null Object supplies a deliberate no-op implementation, while Capability Query reports absence and lets the caller choose a fallback object or policy.
related_patterns_notes.sealed-hierarchy-exhaustive-match: Sealed Hierarchy with Exhaustive Match handles a closed, compiler-known variant set; Capability Query is for open sets whose optional interfaces may arrive later.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy injects a selected algorithm up front, avoiding repeated discovery; Capability Query is useful when the selected behavior depends on runtime support.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: Plugin defines an open extension boundary, and Capability Query lets a host negotiate optional services from a plugin without coupling to its implementation type.
